summary: Jesus warns that disciples will face exclusion and even religiously rationalized violence. His departure, though grief-producing, is advantageous because the Advocate will come to expose the world's error concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment and guide disciples into truth. Their ‘little while’ of sorrow will become joy like birth after labor, and Jesus closes with plain speech, promised access to the Father, and peace within tribulation because he has conquered the world.
whyItMatters: The chapter does not promise escape from trouble. It gives a framework for faithful life inside it: honest warning, Spirit-enabled truth, grief that can be transformed without being denied, direct relation to the Father, and Jesus's prior victory. The Spirit's work is testimony centered on Jesus, not a license for every new claim to outrun him.

context.author: The anonymous Fourth Gospel narrator, completing the farewell teaching before Jesus turns to prayer
context.audience: A witnessing community facing exclusion, grief, delayed understanding, and hostility
context.date: Spoken on the night before Jesus's death within the narrative
context.setting: The final farewell conversation before the arrest
context.literaryForm: Persecution warning, Advocate sayings, sorrow-to-joy metaphor, question-and-answer, and victory conclusion

outline.heading: Jesus warns of exclusion and mistaken religious violence
Departure permits the Advocate's exposing work
The Spirit guides and glorifies Jesus
A little while turns laboring sorrow into joy
Plain speech, the Father's love, scattering, and peace

keyVerses.text: Nevertheless I tell you the truth: It is to your advantage that I go away; for if I don’t go away, the Counselor won’t come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you.
keyVerses.why: Jesus's absence opens a new mode of presence and worldwide mission through the Advocate.

keyVerses.text: However, when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming.
keyVerses.why: The Spirit's guidance is relationally ordered and centered on communicating what belongs to Jesus.

keyVerses.text: I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.”
keyVerses.why: Peace coexists with tribulation because Jesus's victory, not favorable circumstances, grounds courage.

questions.question: What does being ‘put out of the synagogues’ mean?
questions.answer: Aposynagōgos indicates exclusion from a Jewish community, an economic and relational as well as religious loss. The exact institutional form and whether John reflects a single formal decree are debated. Because Jesus and the first disciples are Jewish, the warning concerns painful intra-Jewish conflict, not proof that Judaism as such is hostile to God.

questions.question: How can killers think they offer worship to God?
questions.answer: The verb latreia can denote religious service or worship. Jesus warns that sincere religious framing does not make violence faithful; people can mistake persecution for an offering to God because they do not know the Father or Son. The verse is a judgment on sanctified violence in every community, including Christian violence, not a slur reserved for others.

questions.question: Why is Jesus's departure ‘to your advantage’?
questions.answer: The disciples' grief focuses on losing Jesus's bodily presence. He says his going—through cross, resurrection, and return to the Father—makes possible the Advocate's coming. Through the Spirit, Jesus's presence and witness are no longer confined to one place, and disciples enter a mature mission rather than simply retaining the old arrangement.

questions.question: What does the Advocate do concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment?
questions.answer: Elenchō can mean expose, convict, or prove wrong, with a courtroom flavor. The following clauses define the world's misjudgment: sin centers on refusing Jesus; Jesus's return to the Father vindicates his righteousness despite condemnation; and the world's ruler, not Jesus, stands judged. The Spirit reverses the apparent verdict of the cross through witness.

questions.question: Does ‘guide you into all truth’ promise unlimited new revelation?
questions.answer: Jesus speaks first to disciples who cannot yet bear the full meaning of his death and resurrection. The Spirit does not speak ‘from himself’ but communicates what he hears, glorifies Jesus, and takes what belongs to Jesus. The promise grounds apostolic understanding and ongoing Spirit-led discernment, while its Christ-centered boundaries test claims of novelty.

questions.question: What is the repeated ‘little while’?
questions.answer: The disciples hear the phrase but cannot resolve it. Its nearest horizon is the brief interval of Jesus's death and burial before resurrection reverses their grief; it may also open toward the longer absence before final return. John preserves their confusion so that the promise is learned through events rather than decoded as a timetable.

questions.question: Why compare their sorrow to childbirth?
questions.answer: The image does more than say pain will be forgotten. The same labor that causes anguish produces the child and is transformed by the resulting joy. Jesus does not call grief imaginary; he promises reunion and a joy no one can take. The metaphor is pastoral, not a minimization of traumatic or complicated loss.

questions.question: What changes when disciples ask the Father in Jesus's name?
questions.answer: After resurrection they will pray with clearer understanding of Jesus's completed mission. Jesus does not say the Father is reluctant and must be persuaded by a kinder Son; he explicitly says the Father loves them because they love Jesus and believe he came from God. Prayer in Jesus's name is participation in that revealed relation.

questions.question: Why promise peace after predicting that all will scatter?
questions.answer: The disciples announce understanding and belief, but Jesus exposes their coming abandonment. His realism about failure does not cancel the promise because the Father remains with him and his victory is already stated in the perfect tense: ‘I have overcome.’ Peace is ‘in me’ amid thlipsis—pressure, affliction, trouble—in the world, not denial that trouble exists.

glossary.def: To expose, convict, or demonstrate error; the Advocate's courtroom-like work toward the world.
Pressure, affliction, or trouble; the environment in which Jesus gives peace.
Religious service or worship, used in the warning about violence mistaken for devotion.
